prose.caution: Evidence is thin—only two New Testament occurrences (one in the critical text)—and the two listed senses are really one meaning split by wording.

prose.def: A laying down or founding, used almost always of the 'foundation of the world' (before or since), and once of the conceiving of seed (Heb 11:11).

The word's literal root sense is a "laying down," and Hebrews 11:11 uses it differently for the "laying down of seed" (i.e. conceiving), which is why older glosses like the KJV include "conceive." The most striking outside evidence comes from everyday papyri, where Moulton-Milligan show καταβολή frequently meant a "payment" or financial installment paid through a banker — a commercial sense entirely absent from the biblical "foundation" usage.
prose.caution: The everyday papyri sense of "payment" and the Hebrews 11:11 sense of "conception" both fall outside the dominant biblical "foundation" meaning, so context determines the sense.

prose.def: To render an official ruling against someone, as an umpire deciding against a competitor, thereby depriving them of their rightful prize.
senseLabels: to decide against, condemn, defraud of prize

prose.def: To announce or proclaim something openly and with authority, whether actively or passively, including the gospel, Christ, abstract realities like faith, or forgiveness.
prose.article: καταγγέλλω means to announce something openly and with authority, and in the New Testament it almost always describes proclaiming God's word, the gospel, or Christ himself. The Byzantine text uses it 18 times, and the Berean Standard Bible renders it as "proclaim/proclaimed" in 14 of those (about 93%), with the remaining 3 absorbed into surrounding phrasing. A vivid window into its everyday force comes from a third-century AD papyrus (P Oxy X.1274), where a widow uses the word for the "lamentable news announced" to her about her husband's death — showing the sense of a formal, authoritative announcement. Classical lexica also note a secondary sense "to denounce" (in Xenophon), which does not appear in the measured biblical data.

prose.def: To laugh scornfully at someone (with genitive of person), deriding or ridiculing them with contempt; all three NT uses describe the same crowd mocking Jesus.
prose.article: καταγελάω means to laugh someone down — to deride or mock with scorn, always aimed at a person (in the New Testament it takes the genitive of the person being ridiculed). It appears just 3 times in the New Testament, all in the same scene: the crowd jeering at Jesus when He says the dead girl is only sleeping (Matthew 9:24, Mark 5:40, Luke 8:53). A papyrus letter (BGU III.814) shows the same flavor in everyday life, where a soldier complains to his mother that 'everyone is laughing at me' because his father visited but brought no gifts. In the Septuagint it occurs 16 times, most often translating the Hebrew words לָעַג and שָׂחַק.
prose.caution: The two MSB renderings reflect one underlying sense of scornful laughter; the digest's second 'sense' is a phrasing artifact, and overall evidence is thin (low confidence).

prose.def: To condemn or find fault with someone — whether actively by conscience or passively by one's own contradictory actions or another's judgment.
senseLabels: to stand condemned (passive, by one's actions or others' judgment)

prose.article: καταγινώσκω means to blame or condemn — to note something against a person and find them guilty. In its three New Testament uses it ranges from being condemned by one's own actions (Galatians 2:11, where Peter "stood condemned") to the heart condemning us, or failing to (1 John 3:20-21). A nice everyday parallel comes from a second-century papyrus letter (P Oxy VII.1062), which urges the reader to read a letter soberly and "condemn yourself" — showing the word's use for self-judgment outside the Bible.
prose.caution: With only 3 New Testament occurrences and 2 in the Septuagint, the evidence is thin, and translators disagree on Galatians 2:11.

prose.def: To break or shatter something by force, used of reeds, bones, or other objects; consistently rendered 'break' across all NT occurrences.
prose.article: This verb means to break or shatter something, and all 4 of its Byzantine New Testament occurrences are rendered "break" — a perfectly stable picture across translations. Famously it appears in Matthew 12:20, where the bruised reed is not broken, and in John 19:31-33, where the soldiers break the legs of the crucified men. The everyday Koine papyri show the same physical sense vividly: documents speak of broken house doors, ruined pack-saddles, and head wounds from being struck, confirming this was ordinary language for things smashed or cracked apart.
prose.caution: With only 4 New Testament occurrences, the range is narrow, but the consistent single sense across all sources gives solid confidence.

prose.def: To distribute land, property, or honors by lot or as an inheritance; used of God allotting Canaan to Israel (Acts 13:19, Byzantine text only).
prose.article: This rare verb describes the act of parceling out an inheritance—especially land—so that each party receives an allotted share. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Acts 13:19, where it refers to God giving Israel the land), and there it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word; it is absent from the critical text. The most striking detail is that wherever the word turns up in the Septuagint, the manuscripts show a competing variant, κατακληρονομέω, and Moulton-Milligan note an overlooked passage in Theophylact using it of a general distributing honors and trophies to a city.

Though once thought to be absent from non-biblical Greek, the word actually turns up in everyday Koine documents; Moulton-Milligan cites examples including the phrase "condemnations for envy."
prose.caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the measured evidence for this word is thin.

The New Testament uses it just 4 times, and in two of those cases (Matthew 20:25, 1 Peter 5:3) it describes the kind of heavy-handed rule that leaders are warned against. In the Septuagint it appears 14 times and most often renders the Hebrew כָּבַשׁ ('to subdue'), notably in Genesis 1:28 where humanity is told to subdue the earth.

prose.caution: The lexicons list a mental sense ("comprehend, perceive") that the measured renderings don't capture among the top senses, so its full range is broader than the corpus tallies show.

Moulton-Milligan note it seems to be a stronger form of the more common ἀνάθεμα, and that in Revelation it refers to the very object the curse falls upon.
prose.caution: This is a single-occurrence word whose form is disputed — the critical text and sources favor κατάθεμα, and no clear classical examples are cited.

prose.def: To curse vehemently or devote someone to destruction; attested once in the Byzantine NT (MAT 26:74), absent from the critical text, with uncertain orthographic form.
prose.article: This word means to curse vehemently or call down destruction, an intensified form built from κατά plus ἀναθεματίζω (to put under a curse). It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Matthew 26:74, where Peter begins to curse and swear that he does not know Jesus. Interestingly, the related word ἀναθεματίζω is far more common, showing up in Mark and three times in Acts and frequently in the Septuagint, while this intensive form is essentially a one-off in Biblical Greek.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is absent from the critical SBLGNT text, so the evidence for its range is very thin.

prose.def: To use up or consume entirely — whether spending resources, devouring property, or being consumed by fire (as in Heb 12:29).
prose.article: καταναλίσκω means to use up entirely or consume completely, a forceful compound built from κατά and ἀναλίσκω. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Hebrews 12:29, where God is described as a "consuming" fire, and the Septuagint uses it 14 times, chiefly to translate the Hebrew verb "to eat" or devour. A papyrus letter from the fourth century AD shows the everyday force of the word: a wife complains that her husband "used up" the family's property, while an inscription speaks of interest money being spent on teachers.
prose.caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the sense here rests mostly on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than broad biblical usage.

prose.def: To be a burden or drain on someone, especially by requiring financial support; rooted in the idea of causing numbness or inactivity.
senseLabels: be a burden (not burden someone with one's expenses)
prose.article: In Paul's usage this word means to weigh someone down financially — to be a burdensome expense to the people he ministered among. All 3 New Testament occurrences come from a single author in 2 Corinthians (11:9; 12:13-14), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "burden" two times and "burden way" once. Interestingly, its root literally means to grow numb or torpid (Abbott-Smith notes it relates to a Greek term meaning to grow numb), and it appears in the medical writer Hippocrates; Jerome even thought Paul picked it up as a regional expression from Cilicia.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin: only 3 occurrences, all from one author in one book, so the measured "burden" sense rests on a very narrow base.

prose.def: To signal or gesture to someone (by a nod or motion of the head), beckoning them; also, in classical use, to nod in assent.
senseLabels: beckon or signal by gesture (nodding or head movement)
prose.article: κατανεύω means to make a sign to someone with a nod or gesture, typically to beckon them over. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 5:7, where fishermen signal to their partners in the other boat to come help with the overflowing catch. Greek lexicons note a fuller range — both nodding in assent and signaling by a movement of the head — though the single New Testament use is purely the beckoning sense; Moulton-Milligan find the word in everyday papyri, but admit the readings there are unclear.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, and the papyri evidence cited is described as unclear, so its broader range rests on lexical tradition rather than measured usage.

prose.def: To observe something attentively — whether by eye or by careful mental reflection — so as to perceive, consider, or understand it fully.
senseLabels: (absorbed into context — no discrete English rendering)
prose.article: κατανοέω is built from κατά and the verb for "perceive," giving it the sense of looking closely and taking full note of something. In the Byzantine New Testament its 14 uses split evenly between "consider" (33%) and "look" (33%), with the remaining occurrences absorbed into surrounding phrasing—reflecting how it can point either to careful thinking or attentive looking. In the Septuagint it appears 23 times and most often renders the Hebrew בִּין, "to understand or discern," which fits its core idea of perceptive observation; everyday Koine papyri likewise use it for perceiving or understanding a fact.

prose.def: To arrive at a physical destination or, figuratively, to attain a goal, person, or promised end, typically expressed with εἰς and an accusative.
senseLabels: literal: arrived at a place or destination
figurative: attained to a goal, person, or eschatological end
prose.article: καταντάω basically means to arrive at or reach a destination, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it 13 times across 4 books, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "came" 4 times (67% of the explicit cases) and "reached" twice (33%); in 7 of the 13 it gets absorbed into surrounding phrasing without its own English word. The lexicons stretch it further: it can mean to attain to a goal (Abbott-Smith cites Ephesians 4:13 and Philippians 3:11), reflecting both literal travel and figurative arrival. The most striking outside evidence comes from the papyri, where Moulton-Milligan show that "καταντᾶν εἰς" was a common legal term for property descending to an heir after someone's death.
prose.caution: Septuagint evidence is thin (cited just once or a few times), and the Hebrew counterpart it translates is reported inconsistently between sources.

prose.def: A dulling of mind or senses, a stupor or deep insensibility that leaves a person unresponsive.
prose.article: κατάνυξις describes a kind of mental numbness or stupor — a deadened, unresponsive state, almost like the body part that has "fallen asleep." It appears only once in the New Testament (Romans 11:8, quoting the Septuagint), where it was absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated as its own English word, and twice more in the Greek Old Testament, rendering Hebrew words for deep sleep and reeling. Interestingly, one later Koine source cited by Moulton-Milligan uses it with the opposite-seeming sense of "incitement" or "stimulus," showing how its underlying "pricking" root could pull in unexpected directions.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin and the sources disagree: the literal root means "a pricking," yet the measured biblical sense is "stupor," possibly through confusion with a similar-sounding word for drowsiness.

prose.def: (Passive) to be pierced or deeply stricken inwardly, used of overwhelming emotion such as grief or contrition cutting to the heart.
senseLabels: pierced or stricken to the heart (passive)
prose.article: κατανύσσω literally means to pierce or strike violently, but in its single New Testament appearance (Acts 2:37) it describes people being emotionally "cut" to the heart by what they heard. The Septuagint uses it 11 times across 5 books, where it can render Hebrew words for being stunned, silent, or grieved. A striking parallel comes from an early Christian text quoted by Moulton-Milligan, where a whole crowd was so "cut" by the Holy Spirit's words that the church floor was wet with their tears — and the modern Greek form still means "to be seized with contrition."
prose.caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and varied Hebrew counterparts in the Septuagint, the measured evidence for its full range is thin.

The most telling detail comes from the papyri: this was the standard word for sailing down the Nile to Alexandria, with everyday letters using it for arriving in a city or port by boat. The Majority Standard Bible renders its one occurrence simply with "lake," though the verb itself carries the fuller idea of sailing in and putting ashore.
prose.caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single verse, with most of its breadth drawn from outside papyri evidence.

prose.def: To oppress or wear out; in the NT always passive: to be oppressed by mistreatment or deeply distressed by surrounding wickedness.
prose.article: καταπονέω describes grinding someone down through mistreatment or hardship, leaving them oppressed and worn out. It is rare in the Byzantine New Testament, appearing only twice (Acts 7:24, describing the Israelite being mistreated, and 2 Peter 2:7, of Lot distressed by lawless living), and in both cases it is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than rendered by a single English word. The everyday papyri make the sense vivid: petitioners complain of being "worn down" by tax-collectors (BGU IV.1188), and one document speaks of a desire to thoroughly "worst" one's adversaries in a lawsuit (P Oxy VIII.1101).
prose.caution: Confidence is low: only two New Testament occurrences, both blended into phrasing, so the precise force rests largely on outside papyri evidence.

prose.def: A curse — a pronouncement or condition of doom opposed to blessing; sometimes used concretely of one who bears or embodies the curse.

prose.article: κατάρα means a curse: a formal wish or declaration that harm should fall on a person, standing as the direct opposite of a blessing (εὐλογία). It appears 6 times in the Byzantine New Testament, always rendered "curse," and shows up 35 times in the Septuagint, where it most often translates the Hebrew word qelalah. Everyday Koine documents preserve the same force vividly — a tomb inscription from Phrygia (A.D. 243) warns that anyone who opens the grave will have "the curses" fall on his sight, body, children, and life.
prose.caution: With only 6 New Testament occurrences and the English word absorbed into surrounding phrasing in 4 of them, the measured sense rests on relatively thin direct evidence.

prose.def: To render something or someone inoperative, ineffective, or void—whether actively abolishing it or being passively severed or released from its hold.
senseLabels: be severed or released from (personal, with apo)
prose.article: This is a favorite Pauline verb meaning to render something idle, ineffective, or void—stripping it of its force so it no longer operates. It covers a wide range, from nullifying a promise or law to things that simply fade and pass away, and with people it can mean being released or severed from something (as in Romans 7:2-6, Galatians 5:4). The everyday Koine flavor shows up in the papyri, where a man complains that something "hinders me in my handicraft," and elsewhere it describes an animal or tool being put out of use. In the Septuagint it appears only 4 times, all in one book, translating the Hebrew word for stopping or making to cease.
prose.caution: The measured renderings here are heavily shaped by surrounding phrasing—11 of 27 occurrences carry no English word of their own, so labels like "came" and "away" reflect translation context rather than the verb's core meaning of nullifying or rendering inactive.

prose.def: To count or include someone as part of a particular group or list.
prose.article: καταριθμέω means to reckon someone in among a group — to count them as one of the number. prose.def: To bring something or someone into its proper, complete condition—whether repairing what is broken, preparing it for its purpose, or restoring someone spiritually.
prose.article: καταρτίζω is about bringing something into its proper condition, whether that means mending what is broken (like fishermen repairing nets) or fully preparing and equipping something for its purpose. The Septuagint uses it 13 times across 6 books, most often to render Hebrew רָגַל (10×), the word for sending out scouts or spies, and Moulton-Milligan notes it in everyday Koine papyri, including a temple-list examination in an Oxyrhynchus document.
prose.caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the precise nuance rests mainly on Septuagint and papyri evidence rather than the New Testament itself.

prose.article: This verb means to settle people down — to keep a crowd quiet or hold them back from doing something rash. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 19, where the Ephesian town clerk urges the riotous mob to stay calm and act cautiously. prose.def: A violent overturning resulting in destruction or subversion, used literally of demolished cities and figuratively of the ruin brought on people through harmful disputation.
prose.article: καταστροφή describes a violent overturning that leaves destruction behind. In the two New Testament uses it covers both the literal sense — the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah — and a figurative one, the ruin worked among people through quarreling over words. It is the source of our English word "catastrophe," and a papyrus inscription even uses it for a sudden death, memorializing a woman whose death "cut short the marriage."
prose.caution: Evidence is thin: only 2 New Testament occurrences, both absorbed into surrounding phrasing rather than translated as a standalone word, and one of those (2 Peter 2:6) is omitted in some critical texts.

prose.article: καταστρώννυμι literally means to strew or spread something out, and by extension to lay a person low—to overthrow or slay them. prose.caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and two in the Septuagint, the evidence for this word is thin.

prose.def: To lay down or deposit something (active), or in the middle voice with 'favor,' to do someone a favor, sometimes with a view to receiving one in return.
senseLabels: doing someone a favor (middle, with χάριν)
prose.article: At its root κατατίθημι means to put something down or deposit it, a usage common in everyday Koine papyri—where people deposit seed into the ground or pay money into a bank. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears only 3 times, and the one rendered sense is the middle-voice idiom "to do a favor" (literally "lay up favor for oneself"), as when a governor wishes to please others in Acts 24:27. The classical phrase χάριν κατατίθεσθαι, paying out a favor with a view to receiving one in return, is the most striking feature here, attested both in Acts and in older Greek authors.

prose.def: Paul's ironic label for those who demand circumcision, punning on περιτομή ('circumcision') to brand them instead as 'the mutilation.'
senseLabels: those who mutilate (ironic substantive for Judaizing opponents)
prose.article: κατατομή literally means a cutting or incision into something, and that plain sense shows up in everyday Koine: an inscription uses it for cutting, and a papyrus phrase describes cutting into the ground. Paul uses the word just once in the New Testament (Philippians 3:2), where he turns it into a sarcastic pun: instead of the true 'circumcision' (περιτομή), he labels his opponents the 'mutilation' (κατατομή). The wordplay is the whole point — two similar-sounding words set in pointed contrast.
prose.caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its biblical sense rests entirely on a single sarcastic play on words.

prose.def: To kill or strike down with an arrow or other projectile; used in the Septuagint and in a textually disputed reading at Hebrews 12:20.
prose.article: κατατοξεύω means to strike someone down or kill them using an arrow, combining the preposition κατά with a word derived from τόξον, meaning "bow." It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament and shows up 6 times across 4 books of the Septuagint, where it translates several different Hebrew words. Notably, in Exodus 19:13 it renders the Hebrew verb meaning "to throw" or "shoot," describing how anyone touching Mount Sinai was to be killed; Abbott-Smith notes that some editions read it in Hebrews 12:20 quoting this passage, though leading critical editions omit it there.
prose.caution: This word never appears in the Byzantine New Testament, its supposed New Testament occurrence in Hebrews 12:20 is disputed and omitted by major critical editions, and the listed Hebrew counterparts vary across sources.
